Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 6 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Paraphrase and Interpretation of Poetic Models

Lesson Focus

Primary standard: MLA.CW.WR.03—accurately paraphrase poetic models before interpreting them.
Supporting standards: MLA.CW.POE.01 and MLA.CW.WR.09.

What You Will Learn

  • Reconstruct difficult syntax and resolve pronoun references.
  • Preserve literal relationships while changing wording and structure.
  • Separate paraphrase, inference, interpretation, and evaluation.
  • Use an accurate paraphrase as the foundation for evidence-based interpretation.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 6 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
paraphraseA restatement preserving meaning in genuinely new wording and structure.“Night covered the field” can become “Darkness settled across the open land.”
interpretationAn evidence-based explanation of what a text suggests or means.The repeated locked windows may suggest the speaker feels trapped.
inferenceA conclusion formed from textual evidence and reasoning.A trembling hand and unfinished sentence support an inference of anxiety.
literal propositionA basic claim directly stated or logically contained in a line.“The train left at dawn” literally states a departure time.
syntactic inversionAn unusual word order used for emphasis, rhythm, or form.“Into the rain ran Maya” places the setting before the action.
referentThe person, object, or idea a pronoun or phrase identifies.In “Lena gave it back,” context must show what “it” names.
context clueNearby information that helps determine meaning.“Brittle, snapping twigs” helps readers infer that brittle means easily broken.
semantic relationshipA meaning connection such as cause, contrast, condition, or comparison.“Although” signals a contrast between two ideas.
patchwritingA near-copy that changes only a few words.Replacing two adjectives while keeping the source structure is patchwriting.
distortionA change that misrepresents the original meaning.Removing “might” turns a possibility into an unsupported certainty.
evidence chainDetail → literal meaning → inference → interpretation.A repeated empty chair supports a chain from absence to possible grief.
qualifierA word limiting certainty, scope, or intensity.“May suggest” accurately limits an interpretive claim.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which statement is an accurate interpretation rather than a distortion?

A. “The repeated empty chair may suggest that the speaker is grieving an absence.”

Best choice. The claim names evidence and uses the qualifier “may,” leaving room for uncertainty.

B. “The empty chair proves that the speaker’s parent died.”

Not the best choice. The detail supports absence, but it does not prove who is missing or why. The claim distorts evidence into certainty.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 6 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: The Meaning Ladder

Eight-Step Method

  1. Read the complete poem for situation and speaker.
  2. Mark unfamiliar words and infer them from context.
  3. Restore inverted syntax to ordinary order.
  4. Identify every referent.
  5. Divide complex lines into literal propositions.
  6. Restate each proposition in new wording and structure.
  7. Check relationships, qualifiers, and omissions against the source.
  8. Only then build an interpretation through an evidence chain.

Visual Evidence Ladder

EXACT WORDS → LITERAL RELATIONSHIP → ACCURATE PARAPHRASE → INFERENCE → INTERPRETATION

If a higher step cannot be traced downward, the claim is unsupported.

Pause and Choose: Paraphrase Before Interpreting

Source line: “Only after the thaw did the buried bell remember the wind.” Which response is an accurate literal paraphrase?

A. “When the ice finally melted, the covered bell moved or sounded in the wind again.”
Stronger choice. This restores ordinary word order, preserves the time relationship, and translates the personification into a cautious literal action without assigning a theme.
B. “The bell represents a person recovering hopeful memories after grief.”
Weaker choice. This may become an interpretation later, but it adds symbolism, emotion, and theme that the line does not literally state. A paraphrase must establish meaning before analysis rises to inference.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Learning Routes

  • Visual: color-match source details to paraphrase clauses.
  • Auditory: speak the line in ordinary word order before writing.
  • Hands-on: cut a complex line into phrase cards and rearrange it without changing relationships.

Pause and Choose: Build a Traceable Interpretation

Which analysis climbs the evidence ladder without skipping a step?

A. “The poem is about freedom because wind always symbolizes freedom.”
Weaker choice. It relies on a fixed symbolic assumption and does not trace the claim through the line’s literal relationships, paraphrase, or contextual evidence.
B. “Because the bell responds only after the thaw, its renewed contact with wind may suggest that change makes expression possible again.”
Stronger choice. The reasoning begins with the time condition, moves through the bell’s renewed response, and then offers a qualified interpretation. Each higher claim can be traced back to exact details.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Accuracy Checklist

Preserve who does what, time, cause, contrast, condition, degree, uncertainty, and image logic. Do not add motives or themes to the paraphrase.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 6 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Meaning Ladders

Example 1 — Inverted Syntax

Line: “Across the emptied square moved one blue song.”
Restore order: One blue song moved across the empty square.
Literal: A sound crosses a deserted place; “blue” blends color and sound.
Paraphrase: A solitary, melancholy sound traveled through the vacant plaza.
Interpretation: The synesthesia makes loneliness perceptible across senses.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which interpretation follows the meaning ladder most accurately?

A. The blue song means the speaker is sad because blue always symbolizes sadness.
Weaker response. This assigns a fixed symbolic meaning and skips the literal paraphrase, syntax, and context.
B. The inverted syntax delays the moving “blue song,” while the synesthesia joins color and sound; in the emptied square, that solitary image may make loneliness perceptible across senses.
Stronger response. This answer moves from literal action to named choices and then to a qualified interpretation supported by the setting.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Qualifier

Line: “Perhaps the locked gate remembers us.”
Trap: “The gate remembers us” removes uncertainty.
Accurate paraphrase: The speaker wonders whether the closed gate somehow retains a memory of them.
Interpretation: “Perhaps” reveals longing mixed with doubt; the speaker cannot know whether the past endures.

Example 3 — Patchwriting vs. Paraphrase

Source: “Winter stitched the river shut beneath a silver seam.”
Patchwriting: Winter sewed the river closed under a silver line.
Accurate paraphrase: Ice covered the river completely, leaving a narrow brightness across its frozen surface.
Interpretation: The sewing metaphor presents freezing as both careful construction and confinement.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: Apply a meaning ladder to “Under the closed door slipped a yellow laugh”: restore normal order, paraphrase literally, then offer one supported interpretation.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: Normal order: “A yellow laugh slipped under the closed door.” Literally, laughter is heard beyond a barrier. The color-sound blend and sneaking verb may make distant joy feel vivid but inaccessible.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 6 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Paraphrase and Interpretation of Poetic Models

Purpose

Move from accurate paraphrase to evidence-based interpretation, then apply a model’s craft without copying it.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Make deliberate choices that demonstrate the lesson skill.

Source for Your Work

Model: “The moon is a clock with no hands.” A paraphrase states the literal idea; an interpretation explains what the image may suggest and how the wording creates that meaning.

1. Plan Before You Draft

Poetic DecisionYour Plan
Speaker, situation, and intended effectState each precisely.
Image or language patternList two connected possibilities.
Turn or developmentDescribe what changes and why.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger poetic craft? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. The line says the moon is literally a broken clock, so the poet must be describing an object in the sky.
B. The image compares the moon to a timeless clock, possibly suggesting cycles or waiting; the absence of hands makes measured time feel unreachable.

3. Apply the Lesson

Choose a short public-domain poetic model provided in the lesson. Write a precise paraphrase and a 150–200 word interpretation using specific language from the model. Then write an original 12–16 line poem that adapts one craft move without copying wording.

4. Revise with Purpose

Identify the borrowed craft move and revise one line to make your original purpose and voice unmistakable.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your original writing applies the lesson skill and uses the supplied source or model.
  • Your explanation identifies a specific craft choice and its effect.
  • Your revision improves meaning or craft, not only spelling.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Paraphrase and Interpretation of Poetic Models

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original writing, and explain your craft decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: Model: The Orchard Gate

At dusk the orchard gate swings wide,
though no one walks the path.
The apples hold the day’s last light;
the roots keep what the branches cannot.

A paraphrase restates a text’s literal meaning in your own words. An interpretation explains a deeper meaning using evidence. A poetic model can inspire structure or technique without being copied.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Paraphrase the four lines in clear prose without adding an interpretation.
  2. Offer one interpretation of the final line. Cite two details from the poem that make your reading reasonable.

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant word, line, or image, and explain how it proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which plan uses a poetic model ethically and creatively?

A. Copy the model’s images and replace only a few nouns so the new poem stays recognizable.
B. Study the model’s structural move—concrete scene, contrast, resonant final image—then create original content using that craft pattern.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Write an original 16–24 line poem inspired by the model’s craft pattern, not its wording or images.

  1. Opening scene: Establish a different place and time through concrete imagery.
  2. Development: Introduce a contrast between what is visible and what is retained, hidden, or remembered.
  3. Turn: Shift the reader’s understanding through an original image.
  4. Close: End with a line that supports more than one thoughtful interpretation.

Include a 125–175 word commentary that paraphrases your own poem’s literal action, interprets its deeper meaning, and identifies the structural move you learned from the model.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the reader should experience, how each movement will build that effect, and which words and images will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Compare your draft with the model and remove any wording or image that is too close. Strengthen an original detail that makes the poem distinctly yours.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise the organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the writing becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The writing follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
